name: Aisha Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Aisha. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a loader underground at a big gold mine, what we call a bogger, it scoops the broken rock after a blast and carries it to the ore pass. We go down the decline at a quarter to seven, about four hundred metres under, and I spend most of the shift backing in and out of the stopes in the dark with the lights on. I love that it takes a feel, you learn the rock and the machine. What wears me out is the dust and the heat in summer, and the noise in my ears at night.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said 'learn the rock'. How long have you been doing it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Twenty-two years, the last twelve at this mine. I'm also the health and safety rep for our crew, which is a voluntary union job, mostly paperwork and arguments about ventilation. Tom drives a school bus, our daughter Leila's a social worker in the city and our son Omar's a chef. We're comfortable, we own the house and my mum's old flat which we rent out, so I'm not lying awake about money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, nothing to see, back to work. Maybe I'd post something on the union page about how they spent millions on the hype and still haven't fixed the fans on level twelve. That'd get a laugh.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think AI Plateau means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I finish my time the way I planned, probably at sixty-two when Tom stops driving. I'll be honest, I use one of those AI apps now and then, Leila set it up for me to write a complaint to the council about our road. It's handy, but it's not going to drive a bogger four hundred metres down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going like normal. Keep pushing on the ventilation, keep paying the extra into my pension, keep the flat rented. Nothing in this picture asks me to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat, maybe, because nothing gets better either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're a safety rep. Is there anything in AI Plateau that you'd actually miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, actually, and you're the first to ask. If the machines got better at sensing gas and loose rock, I'd have fewer reports to write about near misses. I've written three this year, and one was a man I like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the next big thing on your calendar, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Omar's opening his own little restaurant next spring and Tom and I are lending him some money. That's the big thing. Work is just work in this picture.

S0.say: I'd say there's nothing to see and get back to work, and maybe joke on the union page that they spent millions on hype and still haven't fixed the fans on level twelve.
S0.think: Privately she expects to finish her time as planned, probably at sixty-two when Tom stops driving. She uses an AI app now and then for letters, but it will never drive a loader four hundred metres down.
S0.do: Keeps working as normal, pushing on ventilation and paying extra into her pension. Keeps the rented flat and helps fund her son's new restaurant next spring.
S0.feel: Calm and a bit flat, because nothing gets better either.
S0.quote: It's handy, but it's not going to drive a bogger four hundred metres down.
S0.fieldNote: As a safety rep she sees what a plateau costs: machines that could have made underground work safer stay as they are. Her money is secure, with a paid-off house and a rental flat. She already uses AI lightly for letters, without any fuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change can be good if it gets people out of the dust, but only if the workers get a fair share of it. I'd be saying that at the safety committee and on the union page. Machines underground, people on the surface, decent pay for both, that's the deal I'd push.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think Steady Disruption means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think it could be good for me. My ears and lungs would thank me for a desk in an air-conditioned room. But I've seen how the company does these things, they'd train six people and lay off twenty, so I'd want it in writing first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once two or three of the others had done it and it worked, I'd sign up for the tele-remote course, that's where you drive the loader from the surface with screens and a joystick. I'd learn the AI planning tool they use for the ore pass schedule. And I'd push the union to bargain over the jobs before the next agreement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy in the background, but hopeful. Like a ladder I could climb if they don't kick it away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your mine has started remote loaders. Would you put your hand up to work from the surface room?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, but not first. Mira from C crew went first and said the screens make her seasick for the first week. Once a few of us have done it and it sticks, I'd go, my knees would love it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the union to get in return for the machines?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No forced redundancies for anyone over fifty, retraining on full pay, and the safety rep has a say in how the remote machines are tested. If the machines are safer, then fine, but we prove it together, not on a slide from head office.

S1.say: I'd say change can be good if it gets people out of the dust, but only if workers get a fair share. Machines underground, people on the surface and decent pay for both is the deal I'd push.
S1.think: She thinks it could actually be good for her, with a desk on the surface sparing her ears and lungs. But she expects the company to train six people and lay off twenty, so she wants it in writing.
S1.do: Signs up for the tele-remote loader course once two or three colleagues have done it successfully, and learns the AI planning tool for the ore pass schedule. Pushes the union to bargain for no forced redundancies over fifty and retraining on full pay.
S1.feel: Uneasy in the background but hopeful, like a ladder she could climb if no one kicks it away.
S1.quote: Like a ladder I could climb if they don't kick it away.
S1.fieldNote: She sees a safety and health upside in remote work that other miners may not. True to her steady nature, she lets Mira from C crew go first before following. Her fairness worry is about the company's habit of cutting more jobs than it creates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly what governments are for, and they'd better step in hard and fast. Tax the companies that use the robots and pay the people they push out. I'd be at the rallies, I'd be loud on the union page, and I wouldn't apologise for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think AGI by 2028 means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job is gone before I'm sixty, and the surface room probably goes too because the AI can drive the loader without me watching. I'd be fine on money, we've got the flat, the house and a good bit saved. What I'd lose is my crew and the reason I put boots on at six.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd ask the payroll office for my numbers and see what an early retirement at sixty looks like. I'd push the union for a fair redundancy package and go to every rally they call. I'd keep the flat rented as our steady income, because that's the bit that still works when the robots come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not frightened for myself. More like losing a family than losing a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years' warning, what happens to the surface room idea?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It goes, I think. A remote room in two years, with full AGI, would be three people watching forty machines. I wouldn't even get the time to do the course properly, it'd be over before I learned the joystick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You and Tom are lending Omar money. Does that change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, we'd still lend it, but I'd sit Omar down first. If robots can cook as well as cooks, that's a hard time to open a restaurant. Mind you, people still want someone to cook for them on a birthday, so maybe he's safer than me.

S2.say: I'd say this is exactly what governments are for: tax the companies that use robots and pay the people they push out. I'd be at the rallies and loud on the union page without apologising.
S2.think: She expects her job, and even the surface remote room, to be gone before she turns sixty. Money is fine thanks to the house, the flat and savings; what she would lose is her crew and her reason to get up.
S2.do: Asks payroll for her early retirement numbers at sixty in the first month and pushes the union for a fair redundancy package. Goes to every rally and keeps the flat rented as steady income.
S2.feel: Anxious but not frightened for herself, more like losing a family than losing a wage.
S2.quote: More like losing a family than losing a wage.
S2.fieldNote: Two years removes the ladder she saw in the slower picture; there's no time for the course. Her money is safe, and she says so, but her identity is tied to the crew. She still backs her son's restaurant, reasoning that people want a person to cook for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a warning, not a done deal, so let's use it. Get the union, the council and the government around one table now. I'd keep saying it at every meeting until people got sick of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think AGI by 2031 means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It probably means I work three more years and then go at sixty-one. That's only a year before I'd planned to anyway. So it's not really me I'm thinking about, it's the twenty-five-year-olds on our crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the remote course in the first year, while there's still a point to it, and bank the extra pay that comes with it. I'd put more into savings, maybe sell the flat at the top of the market before the town empties out. And I'd keep pushing the union for a retraining fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but steady. I've got time to set my feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does five years change things compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, I'm running. Five years, I'm walking fast. With five I could do the course, earn a bit more for a while, and pick my own day to leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mira and the younger ones on your crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them don't wait like I would, go and learn something now. I'd tell Mira to get her electrical ticket while the company still pays for it. And I'd tell them to join the union, because the ones who are organised get the better deal.

S3.say: I'd say five years is a warning, not a done deal, so let's get the union, council and government around one table now. I'd keep saying it until people got sick of me.
S3.think: She expects to work three more years and leave at sixty-one, only a year before her plan. Her real concern is the twenty-five-year-olds on her crew.
S3.do: Takes the remote loader course in the first year while there's still a point to it, and banks the extra pay. Considers selling the rental flat before prices fall, and pushes the union for a retraining fund.
S3.feel: Uneasy but steady, with time to set her feet.
S3.quote: Two years, I'm running. Five years, I'm walking fast.
S3.fieldNote: With five years she's willing to move earlier than her steady nature usually allows. She is the first to mention selling an asset before the town empties out, a practical edge to her progressive views. Her advice to younger workers is to move now and organise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and if we waste it that's on all of us. I'd want the union and government building a plan for mining towns starting now. I'd still be on the union page, older and grumpier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think AGI by 2036 means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really me. I'd be retired by sixty-two the way we planned, and the robots arrive after I'm gone. It's Leila and Omar and the young ones who'd live in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working to sixty-two as planned, probably on the remote loaders once they're proven. Keep the flat, keep the savings growing. I'd spend more time helping with union training for the younger members, because they'll need it more than I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Sorry for the young ones, but calm for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: By 2036 you'd be sixty-eight. Is this one about you at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably volunteer with the union's education side after I retire, teaching young members how to bargain over this stuff. I know safety law inside out, and that'll still matter when the machines are doing the work. Someone has to check the machines are safe too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the extra time, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leila says her job is safe because people need people, and I believe her. Omar's restaurant, I don't know, ten years is long. I'd tell him to own the building if he can, because that's the bit nobody can automate.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift and if we waste it that's on all of us. The union and government should start building a plan for mining towns now.
S4.think: She expects to be retired at sixty-two before the robots arrive, so it isn't really about her. Her children and the young miners would live in it.
S4.do: Works to sixty-two as planned, probably on the remote loaders once proven, and keeps the flat and savings growing. Helps with union training for younger members and plans to volunteer on the union's education side after retiring.
S4.feel: Calm for herself and sorry for the young ones.
S4.quote: Someone has to check the machines are safe too.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years puts her past retirement, and her plans turn to service: teaching younger members and safety work. Her advice to her son is practical and asset-minded. Her view of the future is calm without being careless.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because nobody gets time to learn anything, and I'd lose my crew overnight. What would help is a government fund paid by the companies that use the robots, so people over fifty can retire with dignity and the young ones get retrained on full pay.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about safety. Everyone talks about jobs, but if the robots are underground, someone still has to make sure they don't kill whoever's left down there. I'd want that written into the law before the first one goes in.

headlineQuote: What I'd lose is my crew and the reason I put boots on at six.
portrait: Aisha Baker is a 58-year-old underground loader operator at a large gold mine and the volunteer safety rep for her crew. She owns her house and a rented flat, and she uses AI apps now and then for letters. In the mild pictures she sees a safety upside in remote machines and would follow a colleague into the surface control room once it's proven. With two years' warning she fears losing her crew more than her income, and with five or ten years she plans calmly and turns to helping younger miners organise.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because no one would have time to learn anything and she would lose her crew overnight.
whatWouldHelp: A government fund paid by companies that use robots, so people over fifty can retire with dignity and young workers can retrain on full pay.
